14070:
Salacious describes something that deals with sex or sexual matters in a way that is indecent, crude, or shamelessly inappropriate — and is often designed to shock, excite, or titillate people.

Think of it as a blend of two ideas: something is sexual + it crosses a line of decency in a way that feels dirty, scandalous, or tasteless.

This is not a neutral word. It carries a negative or disapproving tone. When you call something salacious, you're not just saying it's sexual — you're saying it's the wrong kind of sexual. It's the kind that makes decent people raise an eyebrow. It feels like it's trying to be exciting by being crude or scandalous.

It also has a strong gossip-like quality. Salacious things aren't just dirty — they're often juicy in a shameless, tabloid-ish way. Something salacious makes people lean in and whisper.

The word is flexible. It can describe:

Content — a story, a book, a film, a rumor, a piece of gossip, a joke, or a detail that is sexually charged in a crude or scandalous way.

A person or their mind — someone who is obsessed with or delights in sexual scandal and crudeness.

"The newspaper was criticized for publishing salacious details about the celebrity's private life."

Here, the details aren't just personal — they're crude and sexual, and the paper published them in a way that feels shameless and indulgent.

"He told a salacious joke at the dinner table that made everyone uncomfortable."

The joke crossed a line — it was inappropriately sexual for the setting.

"The trial attracted public attention because of the salacious evidence that came out in court."

The evidence involved sexual scandal, and people were drawn to it in a voyeuristic way.

"She had a salacious interest in other people's romantic affairs."

She was obsessed with the dirty details of others' relationships in a way that was unseemly.
The Spectrum: How "Salacious" Compares to Similar Words

Understanding a word is much easier when you see how it sits among its neighbors.

Risqué — just slightly over the line of propriety, but in a playful or cheeky way. Mild. A risqué joke makes you smirk.

Racy — a little bold and sexual, but said with a wink. Still relatively light-hearted.

Bawdy — openly and humorously sexual, in a rough, folksy, earthy way. Think pub humor or Shakespeare's crude jokes. The tone is playful, not shameful.

Salacious — this is where the playfulness disappears. It's sexual in a way that feels indecent, scandalous, and somewhat shameless. There's a disapproving edge to it.

Lewd — similar to salacious, but more raw and blunt. Lewd is crude, explicit, offensive. If salacious is a tabloid front page, lewd is a dirty word scrawled on a wall.

Obscene — the strongest of the group. This is outright offensive, morally repugnant, sometimes even illegal. Far beyond salacious.

So the rough scale goes: risqué → racy → bawdy → salacious → lewd → obscene, from mildest to strongest.
The Most Common Way You'll See It Used

In real life, "salacious" appears most often in journalism and formal writing. The most common pattern is:

"salacious details / gossip / rumors / allegations"

Whenever a scandal breaks — political, celebrity, or otherwise — and journalists are describing the dirty, sexual side of it, "salacious" is the word that gets used. It captures exactly the right idea: the content is sexual, it's scandalous, and there's something slightly indulgent and inappropriate about the way it's being consumed or shared.
One-Line Summary to Lock It In
Salacious = indecently sexual in a scandalous, crude, or shameless way — the kind of thing that crosses a line and feels a bit dirty to even be interested in.
14071:
Salient means most noticeable, most important, or most prominent — the thing that rises above everything else and demands your attention.

When something is salient, it stands out from its surroundings. It's the detail your eye jumps to, the point your mind holds onto, the fact that refuses to be ignored. Think of walking into a completely white room with one bright red chair in the corner. That chair is salient. It's not just present — it commands attention.

This is the heartbeat of the word: salient things don't merely exist alongside other things. They rise above them.

What makes salient special is that it carries two ideas fused into one:

Something salient is both important AND standing out clearly. Most words give you only one of these. "Important" tells you something matters, but doesn't say it stands out. "Noticeable" tells you something is visible, but doesn't say it matters. Salient gives you both at once — it's the thing that is prominent because it matters, or that matters because it's so prominent.

This is why it's such a precise and useful word. When you say something is the salient point, you're saying: this is the one that rises above the rest, the one that deserves your full focus.
How It Feels in a Sentence

Salient is almost always used before a noun, describing what quality that noun has. Here are examples across different situations, with a note on what each one really means:

"The most salient feature of her speech was her honesty." → Her honesty wasn't just present — it was the thing that stood out above everything else she said.

"Let me point out the salient facts before we make a decision." → Not all facts, just the ones that jump out as the most important.

"The salient difference between the two candidates is their economic policy." → Out of all the differences, this is the one that deserves the most attention.

"He made several points, but the salient one was the issue of cost." → Everything else was secondary; the cost issue towered above the rest.

Notice how in every case, salient is picking something out of a crowd and saying: this one, more than the others.

Salient is a formal word, and it pairs most naturally with certain nouns. You'll almost always see it with:

salient point, salient feature, salient fact, salient detail, salient aspect, salient characteristic, salient issue, salient question, salient difference.

You'll rarely hear someone say "that car is salient" or "she is a salient person." It's not used to describe physical things or people in everyday speech. It describes ideas, qualities, facts, arguments, and features — things you analyze or discuss.

Salient isn't a mild word. It doesn't mean "somewhat noticeable" or "fairly important." It sits near the top of the scale. When you call something salient, you're saying it deserves priority attention. It's the thing a thoughtful person would immediately flag as most worth knowing.

Because of this, be careful not to use it carelessly. If you call five different things in an argument the "salient point," the word loses its power. Salient works best when you're pointing to the one (or few) things that genuinely stand above the rest.

Salient does not mean simply "existing" or "present." Not everything that is mentioned is salient. Not every feature is a salient feature. The word implies a judgment — you are saying that out of many possible things, this particular one rises to the top.

It also does not mean "interesting" in a casual sense. Your favorite part of a movie might be interesting to you personally, but that doesn't make it the salient feature of the film. Salient is about objective importance or prominence, not personal taste.
Synonyms — and Why Salient Is Still Better

The closest words are prominent, notable, striking, key, and significant. But here's why salient often beats them all:

"Prominent" leans toward visibility and position — something can be prominent without being important.
"Notable" means worth noticing, but sounds weaker and less urgent.
"Striking" captures the emotional impact but misses the importance.
"Key" captures the importance but misses the "stands out" quality.
"Significant" captures importance but doesn't convey that something rises visibly above the rest.

Salient is the word you reach for when you want to say: this thing is both clearly prominent AND genuinely important — the one that any reasonable, attentive person would immediately recognize as deserving special focus.

To fully understand a word, know its opposite. Things that are salient are not trivial, peripheral, minor, secondary, or inconsequential. A salient detail is one that changes things; a non-salient detail is one that could be left out without much loss.

Salient is a precision tool. It says: of all the things in front of us, this is the one that stands out as the most important and most noticeable. It combines visibility with significance. It is a formal word, used in writing, analysis, professional settings, and careful speech. It almost always describes abstract things — points, features, facts, differences — rather than physical objects. And it works best when used selectively, because its strength is that it elevates one thing above others.

When someone asks you what the salient point of an argument is, they are asking: what is the thing that, above all else, you cannot afford to miss?
14072:
Saline means containing salt, consisting of salt, or relating to salt. When you describe something as saline, you are saying that salt is a defining feature of that thing — either it has salt dissolved in it, or it is made of salt, or its salty nature is what matters most about it.

The "salt" here primarily means sodium chloride — the same salt you put on food — though in scientific contexts it can also refer to other salt-like chemical compounds.
What kinds of things can be described as "saline"?

1. Water and liquids

The most common use. When water has a significant amount of salt dissolved in it, it is called saline water. The ocean is the most obvious example — ocean water is saline because it contains large amounts of dissolved sodium chloride.

A lake that has salty water (like the Dead Sea or the Great Salt Lake) is a saline lake, unlike most lakes, whose water is fresh (meaning it has little to no dissolved salt).

2. Medical solutions

You have likely heard of a saline solution in medical or healthcare contexts. This is simply water with a carefully measured amount of sodium chloride dissolved in it — specifically 0.9 grams of salt per 100 ml of water. It is used to clean wounds, rinse eyes, flush nasal passages, store contact lenses, and in hospitals to deliver fluids directly into a patient's bloodstream through an IV drip.

The reason this precise mixture is used in medicine is that it closely matches the saltiness of human blood and body fluids, so it does not shock or damage body cells.

3. Soil and land

Soil can be described as saline when it contains an unusually high concentration of dissolved salts. This is usually a problem in agriculture, because saline soil makes it difficult or even impossible for most plants to absorb water and grow properly. Saline soils are common in dry or arid regions, or in areas where seawater has flooded farmland.

4. Environments and ecosystems

Entire ecosystems can be described as saline. A saline environment or saline habitat is one where salt is abundant — such as coastal marshes, mangrove swamps, tidal flats, or salty desert pans. The plants and animals living in these environments have special adaptations to survive high salt levels.

5. Taste

Though less common, saline can describe a salty taste. If someone says a dish has a saline flavor, they mean it tastes distinctly of salt — not necessarily unpleasantly, just noticeably salty.
An important nuance: how salty is "saline"?

The word saline does not tell you exactly how much salt something contains — it simply tells you that salt is present in a meaningful or notable amount. Context determines the degree.

  • Seawater is about 3.5% salt by weight.
  • Medical saline is 0.9% salt.
  • A saline soil might have far less salt than the ocean, but enough to harm crops.

What makes something "saline" in any given context is that the salt level is high enough to matter — either to describe it accurately, to explain how it behaves, or to distinguish it from something that is "fresh" or "unsalted."

The opposite of saline water is freshwater — water with negligible salt content, like river water or rainwater.

Since saline is an adjective, it can be modified to express degree:

  • Mildly saline — a little salty (some brackish rivers)
  • Moderately saline — noticeably salty
  • Highly saline — very salty (like the Dead Sea, which is so salty that almost nothing can live in it)

• The doctor injected a saline solution into the patient's arm to keep her hydrated.
  • Farmers in the coastal region struggled with saline soil after the flood.
  • Most fish cannot survive in saline water because their bodies are not adapted to it.
  • The tears running down her cheeks had a slightly saline taste.
  • Scientists found no fresh water on the planet — every body of water was highly saline.

Think of saline as the adjective that answers the question: "Does this involve salt in a meaningful way?" If yes — if the saltiness of something shapes what it is, how it behaves, or how it is used — then "saline" is the right word to describe it. It is a precise, clean adjective that cuts straight to the most important chemical fact about something: it is salty.
14073: Salinization is the process by which salts build up in soil or water over time, eventually reaching levels that are harmful to plants, ecosystems, and human use.

When we say "salt" in everyday life, we mean table salt — sodium chloride. But in science, the word "salt" covers a much wider family of minerals: compounds formed when metals like sodium, calcium, magnesium, or potassium combine with elements like chlorine, sulfur, or carbon. All of these can accumulate through salinization. So while sodium chloride is the most common culprit, it is not the only one.

Salinization happens in two broad ways — naturally, and through human activity.

Natural salinization occurs when:

  • Rainwater and rivers slowly dissolve tiny amounts of salts from rocks and carry them into the soil over thousands of years.
  • In dry, hot regions, water evaporates quickly from the soil surface, but the dissolved salts it was carrying cannot evaporate with it — they stay behind and accumulate.
  • Seawater floods coastal land, leaving salt deposits.
  • Winds carry sea spray and salt particles inland, depositing them on the ground.

Over geological timescales, arid and semi-arid regions (deserts, dry plains) are especially vulnerable to this because there is not enough rainfall to wash the accumulated salts away. The salts just keep piling up.

Human-caused (secondary) salinization is now far more widespread and faster-acting than the natural kind. The main drivers are:

  • Irrigation: This is the single biggest cause. When farmers irrigate crops, they use water that always contains at least trace amounts of dissolved salts. The crops absorb the water, but not the salts. The water also evaporates from the soil surface and is taken up by plant roots — but again, the salts stay behind. With each irrigation cycle, a little more salt is added to the soil. Over years and decades, the salt concentration builds up to damaging levels. This is an almost invisible, slow-motion disaster that has affected millions of hectares of farmland worldwide.
  • Deforestation and clearing of deep-rooted vegetation: Trees and deep-rooted plants act like powerful pumps, drawing up enormous quantities of water from the ground every day. When these plants are removed (for farming or logging), the underground water table rises. This rising groundwater brings up dissolved salts from deep in the earth to the upper layers of soil — right where crops grow.
  • Poor drainage: When irrigated fields do not drain properly, salty water sits in the soil and evaporates, concentrating its salt content in place.
  • Seawater intrusion: In coastal areas, over-pumping of groundwater for farming or drinking can cause seawater to flow into freshwater aquifers underground, making the water and surrounding soil salty.
What does salinization actually do to soil?

This is where it gets very important to understand the mechanism.

Normally, the fluid inside a plant's root cells contains more dissolved substances than the surrounding soil water. Because of a physical process called osmosis, water naturally flows from a region of lower concentration (the soil) into a region of higher concentration (the root cells). This is how plants drink.

When the soil becomes too salty, the situation reverses. Now the soil water has a higher concentration of dissolved salts than the fluid inside the root cells. So water flows in the opposite direction — out of the plant's roots and into the soil. The plant is essentially losing water to the ground around it, even if the ground is wet. The plant desiccates, wilts, and dies, even though it is not short of water in any conventional sense. This is called osmotic stress, and it is the primary way salt kills plants.

Beyond this, sodium ions (from sodium chloride) have a particularly destructive effect on soil structure. They cause the tiny mineral particles in soil (clay particles) to push apart and disperse, breaking down the natural clumping structure that makes soil porous, crumbly, and well-drained. The result is a dense, compacted, crusty soil that water cannot easily penetrate. It becomes almost impermeable — like a brick rather than a sponge.

Salinized soils also typically become hostile to the microorganisms (bacteria, fungi) that normally live in healthy soil and help break down organic matter into nutrients. So the land loses fertility from multiple directions at once.

In severe cases, white or pale salt crusts are literally visible on the surface of the land — a stark visual sign that the ground has become infertile.
What does salinization do to water?

Salinization is not limited to soil. Freshwater bodies — rivers, lakes, and underground aquifers — can also undergo salinization. When this happens, the water becomes unsuitable for drinking, for irrigation, and for aquatic life. Fish and other freshwater organisms cannot survive high salt concentrations. This is a growing problem in many parts of the world where agricultural runoff, drainage, and rising water tables are contaminating freshwater supplies.
Where in the world is this a major problem?

Salinization is most severe in:

  • South and Central Asia — large parts of Pakistan, India (especially the Indo-Gangetic plain), and the Central Asian steppes, where intensive irrigation has been practiced for generations.
  • Australia — where clearing of native vegetation caused massive dryland salinization across the wheat belt.
  • The Middle East and North Africa — arid, heavily irrigated regions.
  • The American West — particularly in irrigated river valleys.
  • The ancient Mesopotamian civilizations (in modern Iraq) are a striking historical example: scholars believe that centuries of intensive irrigation contributed to soil salinization that gradually reduced agricultural yields and may have played a role in the decline of those societies.

Globally, it is estimated that roughly one-fifth of all irrigated agricultural land — the most productive land on Earth — is significantly affected by salinization. It is considered one of the most serious forms of land degradation worldwide.

It is difficult, slow, and expensive to fix, but not always impossible. Some approaches used include:

  • Leaching: Flooding the land with large volumes of freshwater to push the accumulated salts downward through the soil and away from the root zone. This requires both abundant freshwater and good drainage — two things often in short supply in affected areas.
  • Improved drainage systems: Installing underground pipes or channels to carry salty water away from fields.
  • Switching to drip irrigation: Delivering water directly to plant roots rather than flooding fields, which greatly reduces salt accumulation.
  • Growing salt-tolerant plants (halophytes): Some plants, like certain grasses, mangroves, and specialized crops, can survive or even thrive in salty conditions. These can be used to stabilize and gradually improve salinized land.
  • Adding gypsum (calcium sulfate) to soil: This chemical helps displace sodium ions from soil particles and can partially restore soil structure.

However, prevention is far easier and cheaper than cure. Once severe salinization sets in, it can take decades or longer to rehabilitate the land — and in extreme cases, the land may never fully recover.

Salinization matters because it strikes at the foundation of food production. The world's most fertile, most intensively farmed land is irrigated land — and irrigated land is exactly the land most at risk. As global water demand rises and irrigation expands, salinization quietly undermines the very ground we grow food on. It is a slow-moving crisis that unfolds over years and decades, which makes it easy to overlook until the damage is already deep.

In short, salinization is the gradual poisoning of land and water by salt accumulation — a process driven by both nature and human activity, with profound consequences for agriculture, ecosystems, and civilizations.
14074:
To salivate means to produce saliva — the watery liquid that your mouth naturally makes. Your salivary glands (small organs inside your mouth and jaw) release this liquid.

This happens automatically. You don't choose to do it. Your body does it on its own, usually when it detects — or even just expects — food. The smell of freshly baked bread, the sight of your favourite meal, or even just thinking about something delicious can trigger it.

This is why the common phrase "my mouth is watering" means exactly the same thing as salivating — it's just the everyday way of saying it.

The dog began to salivate the moment it heard the sound of the food bowl.
She salivated at the smell of biryani coming from the kitchen.
The figurative meaning — and this is where it gets interesting

Over time, "salivate" took on a figurative meaning. Because salivating is such a vivid, involuntary sign of craving, people started using it to describe intense desire or eagerness for anything — not just food.

When someone salivates over something, they want it badly. They're excited. They're almost desperate to have it, experience it, or get to it. The word carries a sense of raw, uncontrolled longing.

Investors were salivating over the company's skyrocketing stock price.
He was salivating at the thought of finally getting a promotion.
Tech companies are salivating over the new AI chip.

Notice the phrasing: you almost always salivate over something or salivate at something.
What makes "salivate" different from just saying "want" or "desire"?

This is important. "Salivate" is stronger and more vivid than simply saying you want something.

  • "I want that car" — neutral, calm.
  • "I was salivating over that car" — you're almost drooling. The desire is intense, almost embarrassingly strong, and hard to control.

The word also carries a slightly animal quality — because it's rooted in a physical body response. When you use it figuratively, you're painting a picture of someone so hungry (literally or metaphorically) that their body is reacting. It makes the craving feel visceral and real.

"Salivate" is used in both formal and informal contexts, but it leans slightly toward being expressive or colorful language. You'll see it in:

  • Journalism ("Wall Street is salivating over the merger deal")
  • Casual conversation ("I was salivating over those shoes")
  • Commentary and opinion writing

It's never rude or offensive. It's simply a vivid word.

When used figuratively, salivating often implies that the person hasn't gotten the thing yet — they're in a state of craving and anticipation. Once they have it, the salivating stops. So the word is usually about wanting, not having.

He was salivating over the job offer. ✅ (He wants it, hasn't accepted yet.)
He salivated over the offer and immediately said yes. ✅ (He was eager right before the moment of decision.)

ContextMeaning

In its literal sense: your mouth produces saliva, usually because of food or the anticipation of it.

In its figurative sense: you intensely crave or eagerly desire something — money, opportunity, success, a possession — to such a degree that the want feels almost physical and uncontrollable.

The word always carries emotional intensity. If you salivate over something, you don't just like it — you hunger for it.
14075:
Sallow describes a skin color that is a dull, pale, yellowish or yellowish-brown tone — the kind that makes a person look unhealthy, tired, or unwell.

That's the heart of it. Two things are always true when you use "sallow": it's about skin, and it signals something is off about that person's health or vitality.
What Does It Actually Look Like?

Picture someone who has been seriously ill for two weeks, barely sleeping, barely eating, not seeing sunlight. Their skin doesn't just go white — it takes on a kind of murky, washed-out, yellowish tinge. That's sallow.

It's not a bright, golden yellow like a suntan. It's not the glowing warmth of healthy skin. It's a flat, dull, slightly yellow-grey tone — like the color of old paper, or weak tea. There's no vitality or glow to it. It looks almost lifeless.
The Key Nuance: It's Almost Always About Skin

This is important. "Sallow" is almost exclusively used for human (or sometimes animal) skin and complexion. You would not normally call a wall sallow, or a piece of cloth sallow. The word has found its permanent home describing faces, skin, and complexions.

You'll hear it most with words like:

  • sallow skin
  • sallow complexion
  • sallow face
  • sallow cheeks

"Sallow" is never a compliment. It always carries a sense of concern, pity, or worry. When a writer calls a character's skin sallow, they're telling you that character is suffering in some way — from illness, exhaustion, poor nutrition, grief, stress, or simply a life lived without fresh air and sunlight.

It's a word that quietly but clearly says: this person does not look well.

• "After months in the hospital, his face had grown sallow and thin."
  • "The harsh fluorescent lighting made everyone in the room look sallow."
  • "She was once rosy-cheeked, but worry had left her complexion sallow."
  • "The doctor noticed the patient's sallow skin and immediately ordered blood tests."
  • "He had a sallow, drawn look that told her he hadn't been sleeping."

Notice how in every example, "sallow" is doing two jobs at once: describing a color and communicating poor health or hardship.
How It Differs From Similar Words

These words are neighbors of "sallow," but each one means something slightly different:

Pale — simply means lacking color (whitish). It's neutral and doesn't specify yellow. A person can be pale from cold, shock, or their natural skin tone, with no suggestion of illness necessarily.

Wan — pale and weak-looking, often suggesting exhaustion or sadness, but again without the specific yellowish tint that sallow carries.

Ashen — a grey-white paleness, often from shock or fear. Think of the color of ash. Ashen is cooler and greyer; sallow is yellower and murkier.

Jaundiced — medically specific: a yellowing of the skin caused by liver problems. "Sallow" is broader and more general — it doesn't point to a specific medical condition. A person can look sallow simply from stress or fatigue.

Pasty — an informal word for pale and unhealthy-looking, usually very white rather than yellow.

Among all of these, sallow is the one word that specifically locks in that dull, yellow-tinged, unhealthy skin tone.
A Simple Way to Remember It

Whenever you see or hear "sallow," think: "yellowish, dull skin that looks like someone who badly needs rest, food, sunlight, or medical care."

If someone's skin looks like it lost all its warmth and gained a faint, tired yellow instead, that's sallow.
14076: "Sally" has a few distinct meanings, but they are all tied together by one core idea: a sudden, bold, outward movement — either physical, verbal, or mental. Once you feel this core idea, all the meanings click into place naturally.

This is the original and most literal sense of the word.

Imagine soldiers stuck inside a castle, surrounded by enemies. Instead of just waiting and defending, they suddenly throw open the gates and charge outward to attack. That bold, surprise burst outward is called a sally.

The key qualities are:

  • It is sudden — not planned for a long time in advance
  • It is outward — moving from inside to outside
  • It is aggressive — not a retreat, but an attack

"The soldiers made a daring sally from the fortress and caught the enemy off guard."

This is also sometimes called a sortie in military language, and the two words are close in meaning.
Meaning 2: A Witty or Sharp Remark

This is the most common meaning you will encounter in everyday reading, especially in older literature.

A sally, in this sense, is a quick, clever, playful remark — often one that makes people laugh, sometimes one that is a little sharp or teasing. Think of it as a verbal attack, a sudden lunge of wit in a conversation.

It carries a sense of brightness and quickness. It is not a slow, heavy joke — it is a fast, sparkling one.

"Her sally about his terrible cooking made everyone at the table burst into laughter."

"He responded to the criticism with a clever sally that silenced his opponent."

If someone makes "sallies of wit," it means they are throwing out bright, quick, funny remarks one after another.

Note: A sally is never rude or mean-spirited in the deep sense. It is playful — like a light sword tap, not a serious wound.
Meaning 3: A Short Trip or Excursion

A sally can also mean a short journey or outing, especially one that is somewhat spontaneous, lively, or adventurous.

It implies leaving a place you normally stay in — your home, your usual setting — and going out into the world, if only briefly.

"After days of rain, we made a sally into the village to buy groceries and get some fresh air."

"Their little sally into the antique market turned up a beautiful old clock."

This meaning clearly echoes the military one — you are "bursting outward" from your usual place, even if it is just for a pleasant errand or adventure.
Meaning 4: A Sudden Outburst of Activity or Imagination

Less commonly, a sally can refer to a sudden burst of energy, imagination, or action — not necessarily physical or verbal, but mental or emotional.

"In a sally of enthusiasm, she signed up for three new courses at once."

"The essay was full of brilliant sallies of imagination."

Here, the idea is still the same: something that comes suddenly, brightly, and boldly — rather than slowly and carefully.

Every meaning of sally carries these same qualities underneath:

  • Sudden — not gradual
  • Outward — moving from a contained place into open space
  • Bold or lively — not timid or dull

Whether soldiers charge out of a castle, a witty person fires off a sharp joke, a family takes a spontaneous trip to the market, or a writer's imagination leaps forward unexpectedly — in all cases, something is bursting outward with energy. That is the soul of the word sally.

• "A sally" is always a single instance of these things. You make a sally, not a long sally. The shortness and sharpness are part of what the word means.
  • The plural is sallies: "His sallies of humor kept the audience entertained."
  • It is slightly formal and literary in tone, so you will see it more in books than in everyday conversation — but it is a word worth knowing and using because it says something precisely that no other single word does quite as well.
14077:
To sally means to rush out or burst out suddenly from a place — especially a place where you were staying, resting, hiding, or being held back — and move forward with energy, boldness, or purpose.

Think of it like a spring being released. You were inside or held back, and then — with a burst of energy — you go out and forward.

The word has two closely related meanings that build on each other.

The first meaning is the original and more serious one: to make a sudden, forceful rush outward, especially in the context of a fight or confrontation. Imagine soldiers who are trapped inside a fort. The enemy is surrounding them outside. Instead of waiting to be defeated, the soldiers burst open the gates and charge out at the enemy in a surprise attack. That sudden, aggressive rush outward is called "sallying." They sallied out from the fort.

The key elements here are: you were inside something → you burst out → with speed and force → often to confront something or someone.

The second meaning is the everyday, general one: to set out from a place — usually your home, a room, or wherever you were resting — with a sense of energy, purpose, or even cheerful enthusiasm. This doesn't involve fighting at all. It just carries the same spirit of bursting outward with readiness.

For example: After spending all morning getting ready, she finally sallied out to meet her friends. This just means she went out, but with a lively, ready energy — not sluggishly, not reluctantly, but with a kind of forward momentum.
"Sally Forth" — The Most Common Modern Form

In everyday modern writing and speech, you will most often see "sally" used as part of the phrase sally forth. "Forth" simply means forward or onward, so "sally forth" means to set out boldly and energetically into the world — often to face something, accomplish something, or begin an adventure or task.

Examples of how it feels in a sentence:

  • Despite the terrible weather, they sallied forth and completed the hike. (They went out bravely and carried on.)
  • He took a deep breath, grabbed his umbrella, and sallied forth into the chaos of the city. (He headed out into a challenging situation with energy and determination.)
  • After months of preparation, the team sallied forth with their plan. (They launched themselves forward into action.)

Notice that "sally forth" always carries a slight feeling of facing something — a challenge, an unknown, a difficult situation — and going toward it with courage or readiness, rather than shying away.
The Feeling and Tone of the Word

This is important for using it well. "Sally" is not a neutral word. It carries a specific flavor:

It implies outward movement. You always sally out of somewhere or forth into something. You don't "sally" while staying still. Motion — specifically, moving outward from a starting point — is built into the word.

It implies energy. You don't shuffle or trudge when you sally. There's a liveliness, a snap, a readiness to it. Even when used in a gentle context, it suggests the person is going out with spirit.

It implies intention. Sallying is purposeful. You're not wandering out randomly — you're heading out with something in mind.

It has an old-fashioned, slightly literary feel. In modern English, "sally" and "sally forth" are not slang or casual words. You'd find them more in books, essays, or formal writing. When used in conversation today, there's often a slightly humorous or playful tone — like the speaker is borrowing the grand, dramatic energy of the word on purpose, perhaps to make something ordinary sound more heroic. ("Right then," he announced, "I'm sallying forth to the kitchen to make a sandwich.") This kind of usage is intentionally comic because it applies a dramatic word to a small, everyday action.

It's easy to confuse this word with simpler verbs, so here's what separates it:

It is not the same as simply "going out." The word "go out" is neutral. "Sally" adds energy, purpose, and usually a sense of boldness or confrontation with something ahead.

It is not the same as "escape." Escaping implies fear or secrecy. Sallying is bold and often forceful — you're not sneaking out, you're bursting out.

It is not the same as "wander." Wandering has no clear direction or urgency. Sallying is directed and energetic.

If you were to hold the entire meaning in one sentence: to sally is to burst out from a place where you were contained and move forward boldly, with energy and purpose — whether into battle or simply into the world.

Whenever you see it, ask yourself: Who is going out? From where? Into what? And notice that the person is doing so with a kind of readiness and forward energy, not reluctantly or gently. That feeling — contained, then released forward with purpose — is the soul of the word "sally."
14078: Salmonella (noun) refers to a group of microscopic, single-celled living organisms called bacteria. More specifically, it is a genus of bacteria — meaning it is a family name that covers hundreds of related types under one umbrella. These bacteria are shaped like tiny rods, invisible to the naked eye, and are among the most common causes of food-related illness worldwide.

A bacterium is a living, microscopic organism made of a single cell. Salmonella is one such organism. It belongs to the broader family of bacteria that naturally inhabit the digestive tracts (intestines) of animals — including birds, reptiles, cattle, pigs, and even some pets like turtles and lizards. In healthy animals, salmonella often causes no visible symptoms; the animal carries it without getting sick. However, when salmonella enters the human body — particularly through the mouth — it can cause a potentially serious illness.

There are two species of salmonella that matter most to humans:

1. Salmonella enterica — This is by far the more common type and is the main cause of food poisoning. It has over 2,500 subtypes (called serovars), each with slight differences. The most notorious ones include Salmonella Typhimurium and Salmonella Enteritidis, both frequently found in undercooked poultry and eggs.

2. Salmonella bongori — This type is rarer and mainly found in cold-blooded animals like reptiles. It occasionally infects humans but is far less common.
How does it spread to humans?

Salmonella reaches humans almost exclusively through what we eat, drink, or touch. The main routes are:

  • Contaminated food: Undercooked chicken, turkey, pork, beef, and eggs are the most well-known sources. The bacteria live in the gut of these animals and can contaminate the meat during slaughter or processing. Raw eggs can carry salmonella inside the shell itself, because the bacteria can infect the hen's ovaries before the egg even forms.
  • Raw produce: Fruits and vegetables can be contaminated if irrigated with contaminated water or handled by infected people.
  • Unpasteurized dairy: Raw milk, some cheeses, and juices that haven't been heat-treated can carry the bacteria.
  • Cross-contamination: When you use a cutting board or knife to prepare raw chicken and then use the same board (without washing it) to cut vegetables, the bacteria transfer.
  • Animal contact: Handling reptiles (snakes, lizards, turtles), chickens, or other animals and then touching your mouth without washing your hands.
  • Infected people: Someone with salmonella who doesn't wash their hands properly can spread it when preparing food.

The bacteria do not spread through the air or casual contact like a handshake (unless that leads to touching your mouth without washing up).
What does it do in the body?

When salmonella is swallowed, it travels down to your small intestine and colon. There, it invades the cells lining the intestinal wall. Your immune system reacts strongly to this invasion, triggering inflammation. This is what causes the symptoms.

The illness that salmonella causes is called salmonellosis (sal-moh-neh-LOH-sis), though most people simply call it "salmonella poisoning" or "salmonella infection." Symptoms usually appear anywhere from 6 hours to 3 days after eating contaminated food, and include:

  • Diarrhea (sometimes with blood)
  • Stomach cramps and pain
  • Fever (often 38–39°C / 100–103°F)
  • Nausea and vomiting
  • Headache and muscle aches

For most healthy adults, the illness is unpleasant but self-limiting — meaning the body fights it off on its own within 4 to 7 days. The biggest danger during this time is dehydration, because of the fluid lost through diarrhea and vomiting.

However, salmonella becomes dangerous and potentially life-threatening in certain groups:

  • Young children (especially under 5), whose immune systems are still developing
  • Elderly people, whose immune response is weaker
  • Pregnant women, as the infection can affect the fetus
  • People with weakened immune systems, such as those undergoing chemotherapy or living with HIV/AIDS

In these vulnerable groups, the bacteria can break out of the intestines and enter the bloodstream — a condition called bacteremia — and spread to other organs, which can be fatal without medical treatment.

One specific subtype — Salmonella typhi — causes a completely different and much more severe disease called typhoid fever. Unlike regular salmonellosis, typhoid is transmitted mainly through contaminated drinking water and is more common in regions with poor sanitation. Typhoid causes a prolonged, high fever, severe abdominal pain, and can be fatal if untreated. It is considered a separate disease from ordinary salmonella food poisoning, even though the same genus of bacteria causes it.

For most people, treatment is focused on managing symptoms, especially staying hydrated by drinking plenty of water or oral rehydration solutions. Antibiotics are generally not recommended for mild cases because the body handles it on its own, and overuse of antibiotics can cause resistance. However, doctors do prescribe antibiotics when the infection is severe, when bacteria have entered the bloodstream, or when the patient is in a high-risk group.

The most effective ways to prevent salmonella infection are:

  • Cook food thoroughly: Chicken and other poultry should be cooked to an internal temperature of at least 74°C (165°F). Eggs should be fully cooked — no runny yolks if you are in a vulnerable group.
  • Refrigerate food promptly: Cold temperatures slow bacterial growth. Never leave cooked food sitting at room temperature for more than 2 hours.
  • Wash hands frequently: Especially after handling raw meat, using the bathroom, or touching animals.
  • Avoid cross-contamination: Use separate cutting boards for raw meat and other foods; wash utensils and surfaces after they contact raw meat.
  • Avoid raw or unpasteurized products: Raw milk, unpasteurized juices, and raw cookie dough all carry risk.
  • Wash fruits and vegetables: Even produce that looks clean can carry bacteria on its surface.

In everyday language, people often say things like:

  • "The outbreak was caused by salmonella in the lettuce."
  • "She was hospitalized after contracting salmonella from undercooked eggs."
  • "The lab results showed salmonella in the food sample."

The word can refer to the bacterium itself or, loosely, to the illness it causes. In technical and scientific writing, Salmonella is capitalized (as it is a genus name), but in everyday usage, it is commonly written in lowercase.

Salmonella is one of the leading causes of foodborne (food-related) illness globally, responsible for millions of infections and hundreds of thousands of deaths every year, particularly in developing countries where food safety infrastructure is weaker. In developed countries, most deaths occur in vulnerable groups. It is a major reason behind food safety regulations, including meat inspection systems, pasteurization requirements, and hygiene standards in food production — all designed specifically to keep this bacteria out of the food supply and off your plate.

Saltation means a leap, jump, or bound — a sudden movement from one point to another, skipping over the space in between. Think of it as the opposite of a slow, smooth, continuous slide. Instead, it's a sharp, abrupt jump.

This single core idea — a sudden leap, skipping the in-between — branches out into several important fields, each using the word in a slightly different but closely related way.

In its most basic sense, saltation simply means the act of leaping or jumping. If something moves by saltation, it doesn't glide or crawl — it hops. A frog jumping across lily pads is moving by saltation. Each jump is a saltation.

You might also encounter the word to describe dancing, especially styles that involve leaping and bounding movements. A lively, jumping folk dance could be described as saltatory (the adjective form), meaning "involving leaping."
2. Saltation in Geology and Physics (The Most Common Scientific Use)

This is where you'll encounter the word most often in science, and it has a beautifully precise meaning.

When wind or water carries particles — like sand grains, pebbles, or sediment — those particles don't always move the same way. Scientists identify three main ways particles travel:

  • Creep — particles roll or slide slowly along the surface, never leaving it.
  • Suspension — particles are lifted high up and carried along, floating in the fluid (wind or water) for a long time.
  • Saltation — particles bounce along the surface in a series of short, curved hops.

So in saltation, a sand grain gets picked up by the wind or water, flung forward in a small arc, lands, and then bounces up again — over and over. It's a skipping, hopping motion. Imagine skimming a flat stone across water — each bounce of the stone on the water surface is roughly analogous to one saltation event.

Why does this matter?

Saltation is the dominant way sand moves in deserts and on beaches. When you see ripples and dunes forming in a desert, saltation is largely responsible for building them. The bouncing grains also knock into other grains when they land, pushing those grains forward too (this knock-on effect is called "creep"). So saltation is a hugely important process in shaping landscapes.

In rivers and streams, saltation also happens — pebbles and coarse sand grains bounce along the riverbed rather than being swept up into the flow or dragged slowly along the bottom.

In evolutionary biology, saltation refers to a sudden, large-scale change in an organism — a dramatic leap from one form to another, rather than a slow, gradual change over many generations.

To understand this, contrast it with Darwinian gradualism — Charles Darwin's traditional view that evolution happens through many tiny, small changes building up over an enormous period of time. In gradualism, you go from A to Z by slowly passing through B, C, D, E… and every step is small.

Saltation is the opposite idea. A saltationist view of evolution says that sometimes an organism can jump directly from A to D in a single generation — a large, sudden mutation that produces a big, immediate change.

A simple example:

Imagine a population of insects that are all short-winged. Gradualism says they'd slowly grow longer wings over thousands of generations. Saltationism says it's possible for a single mutant offspring to appear with dramatically different wings — a sudden leap.

Is saltation accepted in science?

Modern biology acknowledges that large mutations can and do happen, but pure saltationism as a theory (the idea that major evolutionary changes routinely happen in single giant leaps) is not the mainstream view. Most biologists today accept a picture where gradual change is the norm, but occasional larger jumps — particularly through changes in developmental genes (called "hopeful monsters" in some discussions) — can play a real role. So saltation is a recognized phenomenon, but it's seen as one part of a bigger, more complex picture.

You may encounter the adjective form saltatory in biology/neuroscience. Nerve signals (electrical impulses) in your body don't travel smoothly along a nerve fiber the way water flows through a pipe. Instead, they jump from gap to gap along the nerve, skipping over insulated sections. This jumping is called saltatory conduction — and yes, saltatory comes directly from saltation.

This jumping makes nerve signals travel much faster than they would if they had to travel continuously along the whole nerve. So your body literally uses saltation to think, feel, and move.

The unifying thread across every use of saltation is:

A sudden leap or jump that skips over the continuous, in-between space.

ContextWhat "leaps"?What is skipped?
  • In geology, sand grains leap through the air in bouncing hops, skipping over the ground between landing points.
  • In evolution, an organism leaps to a new form, skipping the gradual intermediate steps.
  • In neuroscience, an electrical signal leaps from node to node along a nerve, skipping the insulated sections.
  • In general use, a dancer or animal leaps through the air, skipping over the ground beneath them.

If you want one mental image to remember this word forever: picture a desert sandstorm in slow motion. You'd see millions of individual sand grains not floating smoothly, and not crawling — but bouncing — each grain hopping up, arcing forward, landing, and bouncing again. That rhythmic, skipping, leaping motion — grain by grain, hop by hop — is saltation.
